vignette:
He is an 18-year-old South Eastern Asian man who comes across as older than his years, with the watchful, contained way he carries himself and the careful pauses before he answers questions. He is single and works as a photographer now, though the word “photographer” does not fully capture how he speaks about his work. He talks about light, angles, and timing the way other people might talk about breathing. For him, the camera is both a craft and a barrier: something that allows him to stay slightly behind the world rather than fully inside it.

His difficulties begin in combat, during a period of his life that he describes in fragments rather than a complete story. He had been young enough to still feel surprised by his own uniform, by how quickly life could narrow to orders, silence, and the next place to take cover. The traumatic event he returns to most often happened during a chaotic engagement that he experiences as both sharply detailed and unreal. He remembers the heat, the pressure in his chest, the sound of shouting and gunfire collapsing into one continuous noise. He describes the moment afterward with a kind of flat disbelief, as if he is telling someone else’s memory: one instant everything is moving, and then a body is on the ground, and he understands with a slow dread that he cannot undo what has just happened. Since then, he has carried the sense that life can split open without warning.

After the event, he does not feel immediately able to grieve. He functions because there is no other choice. He follows directions, keeps moving, and learns to make his face unreadable. But even then he begins to notice that his body is no longer fully his own. He startles at sudden sounds and finds himself scanning exits, rooftops, windows, the hands of strangers. His attention is pulled constantly toward possible danger, as if part of him remains stationed in combat and refuses to stand down. He sleeps lightly and wakes exhausted, often from dreams that leave him disoriented and angry. Sometimes the dreams are not visual so much as sensory: the smell of dust, the taste of metal, the feeling that he is again running but cannot move his legs fast enough.

Back home, ordinary life does not feel ordinary to him. Loud motorcycles, fireworks, slamming doors, even a camera shutter can make his whole body jerk before he can stop it. He hates how quickly his mind jumps to worst-case scenarios, but he cannot slow it down. He watches people’s faces for signs of threat or betrayal and often assumes that others are closer, calmer, and safer than he is. At the same time, he feels detached from everyone around him, as though there is a thin pane of glass between him and the rest of the world. He can be in a crowded room and still feel alone. He says that some days he feels “blank,” and he means it literally: unable to feel pleasure, unable to access the excitement he once had for being out in the world with his camera.

Photography becomes both refuge and burden. He takes pictures because the camera gives him a task, a frame, a reason to look closely without having to explain himself. He gravitates toward early morning streets, empty playgrounds, and faces caught in moments when they are unaware of being seen. Yet even this work is complicated by the war that follows him. Certain light patterns, certain colors of sky, or the sight of smoke in the distance can pull him back into memory with startling force. When this happens, he becomes tense and irritable, sometimes needing to leave a location abruptly, embarrassed by how quickly his breathing changes and how hard it becomes to think clearly. He edits his photographs obsessively, deleting images that feel too sharp, too exposed, too much like what he cannot bear to hold in mind.

He also notices that he has become shorter with people, especially when he feels cornered or misunderstood. Anger rises fast, and afterward he is left with shame and exhaustion. He avoids conversations about the past and changes the subject when anyone asks about his military experience. Even when he wants closeness, he tends to pull away, worried that if he lets people see too much they will either pity him or ask him to explain something he cannot put into words. What stands out most in his telling is not dramatic expression but endurance: the way he keeps showing up, camera in hand, carrying a life that still feels as if part of it is stuck in the sound of gunfire, while another part is trying to learn how to live in the quiet.
